cards.explanation: The answer is that they cross over armed ahead of their brothers. Moses, Israel's leader, tells these men, "All your men of valor are to cross over, armed for battle, ahead of your brothers, the Israelites." Their own land is already settled, but their brothers don't have theirs yet. So these men go first. That's like getting your own keys and then being asked to help carry everybody else's couch, friends.

The answer is False. Moses commands the men of valor to cross over, armed for battle. But he says the wives, children and livestock "…may remain in the cities I have given you…" He even adds, "…I know that you have much livestock…" The families and herds are allowed to stay put.

The word is rest. Moses says the families and herds may remain "…until the LORD gives rest to your brothers as He has to you, and they too have taken possession of the land that the LORD your God is giving them across the Jordan." These tribes already have rest, and their brothers are still waiting for theirs. Moses ties it to two things, the rest and the brothers taking possession, and he doesn't name a day.

The answer is that each man may return to the land Moses gave him. Moses says, "Then each of you may return to the possession I have given you." First the brothers take possession of the land the LORD is giving them across the Jordan. After that, these men go home to what they already have. I'd bet the walk home feels pretty good, friends.

The reason is that the LORD Himself will fight for Joshua. Moses tells Joshua, "Do not be afraid of them, for the LORD your God Himself will fight for you." Joshua is the one Moses is speaking to, and the kingdoms are ones he's "…about to enter." Moses also reminds him, "Your own eyes have seen all that the LORD your God has done to these two kings." So the reason isn't how strong Joshua is. It's who is fighting.

The answer is that Moses asks to cross over and see the good land. He says, "Please let me cross over and see the good land beyond the Jordan…" He also names the pleasant hill country and Lebanon. Right before that, he calls the LORD's works great and mighty. I think wanting to see the land after all of that is a very human thing.

The answer is False. The LORD tells Moses, "That is enough… Do not speak to Me again about this matter." There's no "ask me later" in that. The subject is closed, and Moses is told to stop bringing it up.

The answer is that he looks over the land in every direction. The LORD tells Moses, "Go to the top of Pisgah and look to the west and north and south and east. See the land with your own eyes…" That's four directions to look. Moses can't walk in, but he does get to see the land with his own eyes.

The answer is True. The LORD says, "See the land with your own eyes, for you will not cross this Jordan." Moses gets to look but not to walk in. I think that's a heavy thing to hear, and it's okay to let it be heavy.

The answer is to commission and encourage Joshua. The LORD says, "But commission Joshua, encourage him, and strengthen him…" Moses won't be crossing, but he still has a job to do for the man who will. I think that's a kind way to hand things off. He gets to cheer on the guy who will cross ahead of the people.

The word is inherit. The LORD says Joshua "…will cross over ahead of the people and enable them to inherit the land that you will see." Moses is the one who will see the land, and Joshua is the one who leads them into it. Moses sees it, Joshua helps Israel receive it.
